claim: Most coronary blood vessels of the heart develop from two different progenitor sources—the endocardium (Endo) and sinus venosus (SV).
source: Most coronary blood vessels of the heart develop from two different progenitor sources—the endocardium (Endo) and sinus venosus (SV)—but whether transcriptional or functional differences related to origin are retained is unknown.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing these two progenitor sources.

claim: Shortly after coronary development begins, capillary endothelial cells (ECs) transcriptionally segregated into two states that retained progenitor-specific gene expression.
source: Shortly after coronary development begins, capillary endothelial cells (ECs) transcriptionally segregated into two states that retained progenitor-specific gene expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNAseq data presented in the manuscript showing two capillary clusters at e12 with lineage-specific gene expression patterns.

claim: At e12, Cap2 was exclusively from the SV-enriched sample.
source: Separating plots by sample revealed that Cap2 was exclusively from the SV-enriched sample (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: All but one of the Endo-enriched capillary cells were in Cap1 at e12.
source: All but one of the Endo-enriched capillary cells were in Cap1, but Cap1 also contained cells from the SV-enriched sample (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: At e17.5, there was skewed contribution with a higher percentage of Endo-enriched cells in Cap1 and a higher percentage of SV-enriched cells in Cap2.
source: There was skewed contribution with a higher percentage of Endo-enriched cells in Cap1 and a higher percentage of SV-enriched cells in Cap2 (Figure 1G and H), but no cluster was lineage exclusive, suggesting that additional factors were driving transcriptional heterogeneity.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: At e17.5, no cluster was lineage exclusive.
source: There was skewed contribution with a higher percentage of Endo-enriched cells in Cap1 and a higher percentage of SV-enriched cells in Cap2 (Figure 1G and H), but no cluster was lineage exclusive, suggesting that additional factors were driving transcriptional heterogeneity.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data shown in Figure 1G and H.

claim: In adult hearts, there was a similar distribution of cells into each capillary cluster in both the Endo- and SV-enriched samples.
source: However, unlike the clusters at earlier stages, there was a similar distribution of cells into each of these clusters in both the Endo- and SV-enriched samples (Figure 1j–k), and there were no appreciable gene expression differences between the samples.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data shown in Figure 1J-K.

claim: There is no lineage-based heterogeneity in adult coronary ECs.
source: Thus, we concluded that there is no lineage-based heterogeneity in adult coronary ECs.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the analysis of adult scRNAseq data showing similar distribution of lineages across clusters.

claim: At e12, 40% of Cap1 genes and 3% of Cap2 genes overlapped with the Endo.
source: Indeed, 40% of Cap1 genes and 3% of Cap2 genes overlapped with the Endo, while 47% of Cap2 genes and 1% of Cap1 genes overlapped with the SV (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: At e12, 47% of Cap2 genes and 1% of Cap1 genes overlapped with the SV.
source: Indeed, 40% of Cap1 genes and 3% of Cap2 genes overlapped with the Endo, while 47% of Cap2 genes and 1% of Cap1 genes overlapped with the SV (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The transcriptional identities of Cap1 and Cap2 cells at e12 derive at least in part by gene expression patterns retained from the SV or Endo.
source: We concluded that the transcriptional identities of Cap1 and Cap2 cells derive at least in part by gene expression patterns retained from the SV or Endo.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the overlap analysis of progenitor-specific genes with capillary cluster genes.

claim: At e17.5, there was no clear pattern between Cap1 and Cap2 in the expression of SV- and Endo-specific genes.
source: There was no clear pattern between e17.5 Cap1 and Cap2 in the expression of SV- and Endo-specific genes (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), and there was little to no overlap between Cap1 and Cap2 differential genes and SV or Endo genes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2C.

claim: At e17.5, there was little to no overlap between Cap1 and Cap2 differential genes and SV or Endo genes.
source: There was no clear pattern between e17.5 Cap1 and Cap2 in the expression of SV- and Endo-specific genes (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), and there was little to no overlap between Cap1 and Cap2 differential genes and SV or Endo genes (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: At e17.5, there were 202 DEGs between Cap1 and Cap2, but only 24 DEGs between all Endo-enriched and SV-enriched capillaries.
source: There were 202 DEGs between e17.5 Cap1 and Cap2, but only 24 DEGs between all Endo-enriched and SV-enriched capillaries (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Eighteen of the DEGs between all Endo- and SV-enriched cells at e17.5 were also DEGs between Cap1 and Cap2.
source: Eighteen of the DEGs between all Endo- and SV-enriched cells were also DEGs between Cap1 and Cap2 (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data shown in Table 2.

claim: Sixteen of the 18 shared DEGs have a greater log-fold change in the Cap1 versus Cap2 comparison than in the all Endo- versus SV-enriched comparison.
source: However, 16 of the 18 genes have a greater log-fold change in the Cap1 versus Cap2 comparison (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data shown in Table 2.

claim: The top DEGs between e17.5 Cap1 and Cap2 included hypoxia-induced genes (Mif, Adm, Igfbp3, Kcne3) in Cap1.
source: The top DEGs between e17.5 Cap1 and Cap2 included hypoxia-induced genes (Mif, Adm, Igfbp3, Kcne3) (Tazuke et al., 1998; Lee et al., 1999; Keleg et al., 2007; Simons et al., 2011; Heng et al., 2019) and tip-cell markers (Apln, Plaur, Lamb1, Dll4) (Hellström et al., 2007; del Toro et al., 2010) in Cap1, and flow-induced genes (Klf2, Klf4, Thbd, Lims) (Dekker et al., 2002; Hamik et al., 2007; Kumar et al., 2014; Wang and Zhang, 2020) in Cap2 (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting pathways that could be consistent with localization-driven heterogeneity.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and B, and by citations to prior literature on these genes.

claim: The top DEGs between e17.5 Cap1 and Cap2 included tip-cell markers (Apln, Plaur, Lamb1, Dll4) in Cap1.
source: The top DEGs between e17.5 Cap1 and Cap2 included hypoxia-induced genes (Mif, Adm, Igfbp3, Kcne3) (Tazuke et al., 1998; Lee et al., 1999; Keleg et al., 2007; Simons et al., 2011; Heng et al., 2019) and tip-cell markers (Apln, Plaur, Lamb1, Dll4) (Hellström et al., 2007; del Toro et al., 2010) in Cap1, and flow-induced genes (Klf2, Klf4, Thbd, Lims) (Dekker et al., 2002; Hamik et al., 2007; Kumar et al., 2014; Wang and Zhang, 2020) in Cap2 (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting pathways that could be consistent with localization-driven heterogeneity.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and B, and by citations to prior literature on these genes.

claim: The top DEGs between e17.5 Cap1 and Cap2 included flow-induced genes (Klf2, Klf4, Thbd, Lims) in Cap2.
source: The top DEGs between e17.5 Cap1 and Cap2 included hypoxia-induced genes (Mif, Adm, Igfbp3, Kcne3) (Tazuke et al., 1998; Lee et al., 1999; Keleg et al., 2007; Simons et al., 2011; Heng et al., 2019) and tip-cell markers (Apln, Plaur, Lamb1, Dll4) (Hellström et al., 2007; del Toro et al., 2010) in Cap1, and flow-induced genes (Klf2, Klf4, Thbd, Lims) (Dekker et al., 2002; Hamik et al., 2007; Kumar et al., 2014; Wang and Zhang, 2020) in Cap2 (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), suggesting pathways that could be consistent with localization-driven heterogeneity.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and B, and by citations to prior literature on these genes.

claim: Car4 was specifically expressed in e17.5 Cap2.
source: We next used Car4 to localize Cap2 within the tissue because it was specifically expressed in this cluster and there was an antibody available for immunostaining (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by data shown in Figure 3A and C.

claim: Erg-positive ECs expressing Car4 at e17.5 were located mainly in the right and left ventricle-free walls and dorsal side.
source: Erg-positive ECs expressing Car4 were located mainly in the right and left ventricle-free walls and dorsal side while ECs in the septum and ventral wall were mostly Car4-negative (Figure 3D–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: ECs in the septum and ventral wall at e17.5 were mostly Car4-negative.
source: Erg-positive ECs expressing Car4 were located mainly in the right and left ventricle-free walls and dorsal side while ECs in the septum and ventral wall were mostly Car4-negative (Figure 3D–F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3D-F.

claim: Cap1 at e17.5 localizes primarily to the septum and ventral wall.
source: This indicated that Cap1 localizes primarily to the septum and ventral wall and Cap2 to the remaining walls of the ventricle.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the Car4 staining pattern and its specific expression in Cap2.

claim: Cap2 at e17.5 localizes to the remaining walls of the ventricle (not septum and ventral wall).
source: This indicated that Cap1 localizes primarily to the septum and ventral wall and Cap2 to the remaining walls of the ventricle.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the Car4 staining pattern and its specific expression in Cap2.

claim: Kcne3 was specific to e17.5 Cap1.
source: The Kcne3 pattern provided further support for this localization because it was specific to Cap1, and in situ hybridization revealed specific septal and ventral expression (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: In situ hybridization for Kcne3 revealed specific septal and ventral expression at e14.5.
source: The Kcne3 pattern provided further support for this localization because it was specific to Cap1, and in situ hybridization revealed specific septal and ventral expression (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Endo-lineage cells outside the septum at e17.5 were more likely to express Car4 than those in the septum (on average, 23% outside septum versus 4% inside septum).
source: However, the opposite was true. Endo-lineage cells outside the septum were more likely to express Car4 than those in the septum (on average, 23% outside septum versus 4% inside septum) (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantification data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Car4 is broadly expressed in all adult capillary populations.
source: To test this, we examined Car4 in the adult dataset, and found that it is broadly expressed in all adult capillary populations (Figure 3H).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by scRNAseq data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Septum ECs had become positive for Car4 in adult hearts.
source: Additionally, immunostaining confirmed that septum ECs had become positive for Car4 in adults (Figure 3I, Table 3).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3I and Table 3.

claim: There was no difference in proliferation between Endo- and SV-enriched ECs in adult hearts following IR injury.
source: This analysis found no difference between the lineages (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The outer wall showed a consistent, though non-significant, increase in EC proliferation over the inner wall following IR injury.
source: In contrast to the lineage comparison, the outer wall showed a consistent, though non-significant, increase in EC proliferation over the inner wall, both within and adjacent to the injury site and regardless of lineage, indicating that this injury and proliferation assay can reveal differences (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Approximately 69% of large arteries (n = 32) identified in the injured regions contained at least one EdU-positive EC.
source: Approximately 69% of large arteries (n = 32) identified in the injured regions that we analyzed (as indicated in Figure 4B) contained at least one EdU-positive EC, and there was a significantly higher rate of EdU-positive ECs in the arteries of injured compared to uninjured hearts (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: There was a significantly higher rate of EdU-positive ECs in the arteries of injured compared to uninjured hearts.
source: Approximately 69% of large arteries (n = 32) identified in the injured regions that we analyzed (as indicated in Figure 4B) contained at least one EdU-positive EC, and there was a significantly higher rate of EdU-positive ECs in the arteries of injured compared to uninjured hearts (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The majority of human Cap1 cells mapped to mouse Cap1.
source: This showed close concordance between the two species (Figure 5F and G). With respect to the two capillary clusters that were extensively studied above, the majority of human Cap1 cells mapped to mouse Cap1, while the majority of human Cap2 cells mapped to mouse Cap2 (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by reference mapping data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The majority of human Cap2 cells mapped to mouse Cap2.
source: This showed close concordance between the two species (Figure 5F and G). With respect to the two capillary clusters that were extensively studied above, the majority of human Cap1 cells mapped to mouse Cap1, while the majority of human Cap2 cells mapped to mouse Cap2 (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by reference mapping data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Mouse Cap2 almost completely mapped to human Cap2.
source: When assigning mouse cells to human clusters, mouse Cap2 almost completely mapped to human Cap2, while mouse Cap1 mapped substantially to human Cap1, Cap2, and Art3 (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by reference mapping data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Mouse Cap1 mapped substantially to human Cap1, Cap2, and Art3.
source: When assigning mouse cells to human clusters, mouse Cap2 almost completely mapped to human Cap2, while mouse Cap1 mapped substantially to human Cap1, Cap2, and Art3 (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by reference mapping data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Human Cap1 displayed patterns indicative of experiencing low blood flow conditions and potentially increased hypoxia (lower LIMS2, THBD, KLF2, KLF4 and higher ADM, IGFBP3, KCNE3, LAMB1).
source: Analyzing specific gene expression revealed several enriched genes shared between corresponding mouse and human capillary clusters (including KIT, ODC1, CD300LG, RAMP3), and showed that human Cap1, like its mouse correlate, displayed patterns indicative of experiencing low blood flow conditions and potentially increased hypoxia, that is, lower LIMS2, THBD, KLF2, KLF4 and higher ADM, IGFBP3, KCNE3, LAMB1 (Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: CA4 (the human homolog of mouse Car4) was not differentially expressed between human Cap1 and Cap2.
source: Notably, CA4 (the human homolog of mouse Car4) was not differentially expressed between human Cap1 and Cap2.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the human scRNAseq data.

claim: There was a statistically significant difference in the amount of TINAGL1 RNA detection between the septum and the heart walls in both an 18-week and a 20-week gestational heart, with the septum having dramatically lower expression.
source: This revealed a statistically significant difference in the amount of TINAGL1 RNA detection between the septum and the heart walls in both an 18-week and a 20-week gestational heart, with the septum having dramatically lower expression (Figure 5J–K).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by in situ hybridization quantification data shown in Figure 5J-K.

claim: The difference in TINAGL1 expression was especially pronounced between the septum and the right ventricular free wall.
source: This difference was especially pronounced between the septum and the right ventricular free wall, similar to the Car4 pattern in mouse (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by in situ hybridization quantification data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: There was no difference in TINAGL1 detection between the ventral and dorsal walls in human fetal hearts.
source: In contrast to mouse Car4, there was no difference in TINAGL1 detection between the ventral and dorsal walls (Figure 5K).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by in situ hybridization quantification data shown in Figure 5K.

claim: A higher percentage of human Cap1 than Cap2 cells matched to the putative mouse septal ECs (35% of Cap1 cells versus 14% of Cap2 cells).
source: When using the Label Transfer workflow to specifically map the putative mouse septal ECs to the human data, a higher percentage of human Cap1 than Cap2 cells matched to this septal EC group (35% of Cap1 cells versus 14% of Cap2 cells) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by reference mapping data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Mouse cells mapped to all three human artery clusters.
source: Instead, mouse cells mapped to all three human artery clusters (Figure 6a).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by reference mapping data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A high proportion of human Art3 cells matched mouse capillaries.
source: This is because: (1) Art3 was unique among the human artery clusters in that a high proportion of Art3 cells matched mouse capillaries (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by reference mapping data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Trajectory analysis with RNA velocity, Slingshot, and PAGA indicated a transition from human Art3 -> Art2 -> Art1.
source: (2) Trajectory analysis with RNA velocity (La Manno et al., 2018), Slingshot (Street et al., 2018), and partition-based graph abstraction (PAGA) (Wolf et al., 2019) indicated a transition from human Art3 -> Art2 -> Art1 (Figure 6B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by trajectory analysis data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Almost no adult human artery ECs mapped to Art3.
source: (3) Comparing the fetal dataset with a publicly available adult dataset (Litviňuková et al., 2020) showed that almost no adult human artery ECs mapped to Art3, which would be predicted if Art3 were an immature developmental state (Figure 6C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by reference mapping data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: PAGA and Slingshot identified connections between human Cap1 and Art3 and Cap2 and Art2.
source: Two common methods for estimating trajectories, PAGA and Slingshot, identified connections between human Cap1 and Art3 and Cap2 and Art2 (Figure 6B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by trajectory analysis data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: RNA velocity suggested directionality going from the capillaries into arteries in human.
source: RNA velocity suggested directionality going from the capillaries into arteries (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by RNA velocity analysis data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Several genes are specifically co-expressed in human Cap1 and Art3 (including CXCR7, MCAM, and TNFAIP8L1, PGF).
source: This is supported by the observation that several genes are specifically co-expressed in Cap1 and Art3 (including CXCR7, MCAM, and TNFAIP8L1, PGF) or in Cap2 and Art2 (including TINAGL1, SLC9A3R2, SGK1, THBD, LIMS2, CALCRL), some of which were shared with mouse (Figures 5H and 6D, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Several genes are specifically co-expressed in human Cap2 and Art2 (including TINAGL1, SLC9A3R2, SGK1, THBD, LIMS2, CALCRL).
source: This is supported by the observation that several genes are specifically co-expressed in Cap1 and Art3 (including CXCR7, MCAM, and TNFAIP8L1, PGF) or in Cap2 and Art2 (including TINAGL1, SLC9A3R2, SGK1, THBD, LIMS2, CALCRL), some of which were shared with mouse (Figures 5H and 6D, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: SCENIC analysis implicated SOX17 as being strongly enriched in developing artery ECs.
source: The SCENIC package (Aibar et al., 2017), which uses gene expression information to identify transcription factor 'regulons' present in cells, implicated SOX17 as being strongly enriched in developing artery ECs (Figure 7B), which is consistent with previous reports on artery development (Corada et al., 2013; González-Hernández et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by SCENIC analysis data shown in Figure 7B and by citations to prior literature.

claim: Transcription factors of potential importance that have not been previously implicated in artery development were PRDM16 and GATA2.
source: Transcription factors of potential importance that have not been previously implicated in artery development were PRDM16 and GATA2 (Figure 7B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by SCENIC analysis data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The IRF6 regulon was specific to the most mature artery population.
source: Interestingly, the IRF6 regulon was specific to the most mature population suggesting a potential role in artery maturation (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by SCENIC analysis data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: All of the transcription factor regulons identified in human artery ECs were similarly enriched in mouse artery cells.
source: All of these regulons were similarly enriched in mouse artery cells (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by SCENIC analysis data shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Human developing coronary arteries expressed a GABA receptor, GABBR2, which was enriched in Art2.
source: Interestingly, these included a GABA receptor, GABBR2, which was enriched in Art2, and a Glutamate receptor, GRIA2, which was is enriched in Art1.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the human scRNAseq data.

claim: Human developing coronary arteries expressed a Glutamate receptor, GRIA2, which was enriched in Art1.
source: Interestingly, these included a GABA receptor, GABBR2, which was enriched in Art2, and a Glutamate receptor, GRIA2, which was is enriched in Art1.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the human scRNAseq data.

claim: The human cells expressing GABBR2 also co-expressed SLC6A6, a transporter that imports the GABBR2 ligand into cells.
source: The human cells expressing GABBR2 also co-expressed SLC6A6, a transporter that imports the GABBR2 ligand into cells (Tomi et al., 2008; Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by gene expression data shown in Figure 7D and by citation to prior literature.

claim: GJA5-positive ECs (marking Art1) are in a small number of large arteries always covered with smooth muscle in human fetal hearts.
source: We found that GJA5-positive ECs, marking Art1, are in a small number of large arteries always covered with smooth muscle, while GJA5-negative/GJA4-positive ECs, marking Art2 and Art3, are numerous and in some cases not covered with smooth muscle (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: GJA5-negative/GJA4-positive ECs (marking Art2 and Art3) are numerous and in some cases not covered with smooth muscle in human fetal hearts.
source: We found that GJA5-positive ECs, marking Art1, are in a small number of large arteries always covered with smooth muscle, while GJA5-negative/GJA4-positive ECs, marking Art2 and Art3, are numerous and in some cases not covered with smooth muscle (Figure 7E and F).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7E and F.

claim: BmxCreER specifically labels a high percentage of the Endo (94.44% of Endo cells labeled at e12.5), but does not mark the SV (3.61% of SV cells labeled at e12.5).
source: A tamoxifen-inducible BmxCreER (Ehling et al., 2013) mouse was crossed with the RosatdTomato Cre reporter, which specifically labels a high percentage of the Endo (94.44% of Endo cells labeled at e12.5), but does not mark the SV (3.61% of SV cells labeled at e12.5) (D'Amato et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work characterizing the BmxCreER line.

claim: The major progenitor sources for coronary endothelial cells (ECs) in mice are the sinus venosus (SV), the venous inflow tract of the developing heart, and the endocardium (Endo), the inner lining of the heart ventricles.
source: The major progenitor sources for coronary endothelial cells (ECs) in mice are the sinus venosus (SV), the venous inflow tract of the developing heart, and the endocardium (Endo), the inner lining of the heart ventricles (Red-Horse et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2014; Tian et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2017; Su et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing these progenitor sources.

claim: ECs begin to migrate from both the SV and Endo at embryonic day 11.5.
source: ECs begin to migrate from both these sources at embryonic day 11.5.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge of coronary development timing.

claim: The SV contributes vessels to the outer myocardial wall in adults.
source: These two sources eventually localize to largely complimentary regions in adults: the SV contributes vessels to the outer myocardial wall and the Endo contributes vessels to the inner myocardial wall and the septum (Red-Horse et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2014; He et al., 2014; Tian et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on coronary lineage localization.

claim: The Endo contributes vessels to the inner myocardial wall and the septum in adults.
source: These two sources eventually localize to largely complimentary regions in adults: the SV contributes vessels to the outer myocardial wall and the Endo contributes vessels to the inner myocardial wall and the septum (Red-Horse et al., 2010; Wu et al., 2012; Chen et al., 2014; He et al., 2014; Tian et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on coronary lineage localization.

claim: Initial angiogenesis from the SV or Endo is guided by different signaling factors.
source: Initial angiogenesis from the SV or Endo is guided by different signaling factors (Wu et al., 2012; Arita et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2014; Su et al., 2018; Payne et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on signaling in coronary angiogenesis.

claim: In circumstances where SV angiogenesis is stunted, Endo-derived vasculature can expand into the outer wall to compensate for the vessel loss.
source: However, in circumstances where SV angiogenesis is stunted, Endo-derived vasculature can expand into the outer wall to compensate for the vessel loss (Sharma et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work demonstrating compensatory angiogenesis.

claim: Over the course of development, transcriptional heterogeneity in coronary ECs is first influenced by lineage, then by location, until both lineage- and location-based heterogeneity disappear in the static adult heart.
source: Thus, over the course of development, transcriptional heterogeneity in coronary ECs is first influenced by lineage, then by location, until heterogeneity declines in the homeostatic adult heart.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, based on the integration of all scRNAseq and histological data.

claim: Human coronary development closely matches that in mice.
source: Finally, scRNAseq of developing human coronary vessels indicated that the human heart followed similar principles.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the comparison of human and mouse scRNAseq datasets.

claim: The local environment, rather than lineage, regulates capillary responses to injury in adult hearts, at least with respect to EC proliferation in the days after injury.
source: These data support the notion that the local environment, rather than lineage, regulates capillary responses to injury in adult hearts, at least with respect to EC proliferation in the days after injury.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the IR injury experiment showing no lineage-based difference in proliferation.

claim: 28% of fetal capillary cells are Cap1 versus 6% of adult capillary cells in human.
source: Reference mapping from the fetal to adult human datasets also revealed a notable reduction in Cap1 cells (28% of fetal capillary cells are Cap1 versus 6% of adult capillary cells) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by reference mapping data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The small percentage of adult human coronary ECs mapping to the fetal Cap1 cluster indicates that developmental states related to flow and oxygenation converge in humans.
source: The small percentage of adult human coronary ECs mapping to the fetal Cap1 cluster, as well as the spatial overlap between cells mapping to Cap1 and Cap2 in the adult UMAP reduction, indicates that these developmental states related to flow and oxygenation also converge in humans.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the reference mapping analysis comparing fetal and adult human datasets.

claim: In both mouse and human, two distinct subtypes of capillary cells at different locations in the developing heart initially produce two subtypes of artery cells, one of which eventually matures into the other.
source: From these data, we propose a model where, in both mouse and human, two distinct subtypes of capillary cells at different locations in the developing heart initially produce two subtypes of artery cells, one of which eventually matures into the other (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on trajectory analysis and gene expression patterns.

claim: Art1 represents artery ECs in larger, more proximal branches in human.
source: This supports the conclusion that Art1 represents artery ECs in larger, more proximal branches, and Art2 and Art3 are smaller arterioles (Figure 7G).
evidence: This conclusion is based on in situ hybridization data showing GJA5 expression patterns.

claim: Art2 and Art3 are smaller arterioles in human.
source: This supports the conclusion that Art1 represents artery ECs in larger, more proximal branches, and Art2 and Art3 are smaller arterioles (Figure 7G).
evidence: This conclusion is based on in situ hybridization data showing GJA5 expression patterns.
